pos: n. (the Seventeen Provinces of the Low Countries, which gave the Reformation its first martyrs and its most carefully confessed church)
etymology: Dutch Nederlanden, the low lands, from neder, low, and land; Latin Belgium Foederatum for the northern union.
biblical_def: The Netherlands is the land in which the Reformation was resisted earliest, confessed most exactly, and finally established by a war of eighty years. Luther's books reached Antwerp within two years of 1517, and the first men put to death anywhere for the Reformation were the Augustinians Hendrik Voes and Jan van Esch, burned at Brussels on 1 July 1523, of whom Luther wrote his first hymn. Charles V governed the provinces as his own patrimony and issued placards against heresy whose severity was unmatched in Europe; thousands died under them, Anabaptists more than any other party. Out of that furnace came the Belgic Confession, written by Guido de Bres in 1561 and thrown over the wall of Tournai castle with a letter to the king; the image-breaking of 1566; the revolt from 1568; the Union of Utrecht of 1579, by which the seven northern provinces bound themselves together while the southern provinces returned to Spain by the Union of Arras; the Synod of Dort of 1618 and 1619, where the Reformed churches of Europe answered Arminianism; and the States Bible of 1637. The dictionary enters the Netherlands because no other land shows so plainly that a confession, a synod and a translation are what a persecuted church must produce if it means to outlive the persecution.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a placard as a written or printed edict published; a confession as a formulary of the articles of faith; a synod as a council of ecclesiastics; and a province as a country belonging to a kingdom.
webster_full: PLACARD, n. An edict; a declaration; a manifesto; a written or printed paper posted in a public place.
CONFESSION, n. A formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised; a profession of belief.
SYNOD, n. A council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion; an assembly of ministers and elders.
PROVINCE, n. A country belonging to a kingdom or state, either by conquest or colonization; a region of country.
MARTYR, n. One who by his death bears witness to the truth of the gospel; one who suffers death for his religion.

corruption_summary: The Seventeen Provinces of the Low Countries, where the Reformation's first martyrs died in 1523 and the Belgic Confession, the Synod of Dort and the States Bible were produced. (Distinct from the Spanish Netherlands, the southern provinces that returned to Habsburg obedience by the Union of Arras in 1579.)
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the persecution conducted as public administration, and the Netherlands under the placards is its largest instance in the sixteenth century. The edicts were printed, numbered and posted, the commissioners were salaried, the procedure was regular, and the toll ran into thousands. The dictionary records that the Anabaptists bore the heaviest share of it, and that the Reformed who later held the provinces did not always remember this. “the souls of them that were slain for the word of God” (Rev 6:9) is a company larger than any one party's martyrology.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a church under fire must build what outlasts it, which is what these provinces did. They wrote a confession, bound their churches in a synodical order, and put the Scriptures into Dutch; and the officers who did it were charged to “feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28). The warning side is also theirs: a victorious church must still “speak the same thing” (1Co 1:10), and within forty years of the revolt the Dutch were in a quarrel over grace that Dort had to settle.

pos: n. (the chief province of the Dutch republic, whose wealth paid for the revolt and whose regents sheltered the Arminian party)
etymology: Dutch Holland, from Middle Dutch holtland, woodland, or hol land, hollow land, for its peat and marsh.
biblical_def: Holland was the richest of the Seventeen Provinces and the one that set the terms of the Dutch Reformation. Its towns, Amsterdam, Leiden, Haarlem, Delft, Dordrecht, Gouda and Rotterdam, held the trade, the shipping and the tax base, so that the province paid much of the cost of the war against Spain and expected a corresponding voice. Its Reformed churches were planted from exile congregations and the preaching of returned refugees, and Leiden's university, founded in 1575 as the republic's thanksgiving for its deliverance, became the most important Reformed faculty in Europe. Holland is also where the Arminian controversy was fought, and the shape of the quarrel was provincial as much as doctrinal: Jacobus Arminius taught at Leiden, the Remonstrants had their strength among the town regents, and the Advocate of Holland, Johan van Oldenbarnevelt, held that the civil authority of the province should decide what the churches might require. The Synod of Dort of 1618 and 1619 decided against him on both counts, and Oldenbarnevelt was executed in 1619. The dictionary enters Holland because the Remonstrant controversy was carried by a magistracy that wanted the keys, and because the Canons of Dort are the church's answer to a theology and to a magistrate at once.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a regent as one who governs; an advocate as one who pleads the cause of another; a remonstrance as a strong representation against something; and a canon as a law or rule of doctrine.
webster_full: REGENT, n. A governor; a ruler; one invested with vicarious authority; one who governs a kingdom in the minority of the king.
ADVOCATE, n. One who pleads the cause of another in a court; one who defends or vindicates.
REMONSTRANCE, n. Show; discovery; a strong representation of reasons against a measure; expostulation.
CANON, n. In ecclesiastical affairs, a law or rule of doctrine or discipline enacted by a council.
KEY, n. An instrument for shutting or opening a lock; figuratively, the power of binding and loosing.

corruption_summary: Chief province of the Dutch republic, home of Leiden's university and of the Remonstrant party among its town regents, answered by the Synod of Dort.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is Arminianism, and Holland is where it was first organised as a party with civil protection. The Remonstrance of 1610 asked for a conditional election, a universal atonement, a grace that may be finally resisted and a perseverance left uncertain, and the regents of Holland defended the men who taught it on the ground that the province, not the synod, should settle what a minister may hold. Scripture answers the doctrine directly: “So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy” (Rom 9:16), and “No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him” (Joh 6:44).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the church's own authority to examine its ministers, which is what the regents of Holland contested and Dort maintained. The overseers of a congregation are set by the Holy Ghost to “feed the church of God” (Act 20:28), and a provincial advocate holds no such commission. The standard by which the Remonstrance was judged was not the synod's dignity but the text, and “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) is how the Canons proceed, article by article.

pos: n. (the island province at the mouth of the Scheldt, the strictest of the Dutch provinces, where the Nadere Reformatie began)
etymology: Dutch Zeeland, sea-land, from zee, the sea, and land; the province is a group of islands and drowned polders.
biblical_def: Zeeland was the smallest and most exposed of the provinces that made the Dutch republic, a scatter of islands behind dykes at the mouth of the Scheldt, and it was the hardest of them in doctrine and discipline. Flushing and Brielle were the first towns taken for the revolt in 1572 by the Sea Beggars, and Zeeland's seamen kept the water route by which Antwerp could be strangled and Leiden relieved. Its churches were planted largely by returning exiles from London and Emden, who brought back a worked church order and a severity about discipline the great trading towns of Holland never accepted; Zeeland's delegates at Dort were among the strictest, and the province resisted the Holland regents' claim to govern the church. Its most lasting contribution was made at Middelburg, where Willem Teellinck, minister there from 1613, began the movement called the Nadere Reformatie, the further reformation: a demand that the doctrine already confessed be pressed into household practice, personal godliness and the Sabbath, on the ground that a nation with a sound confession may still be an ungodly nation. The dictionary enters Zeeland because that demand is the right one to make of a church that has won its arguments.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a dyke as a bank to prevent inundation; discipline as instruction and government; godliness as piety toward God; and practice as the habitual performance of duty.
webster_full: DYKE, n. A ditch; a channel for water; a mound of earth or stone to prevent low lands from being inundated by the sea.
DISCIPLINE, n. Instruction and government; subjection to rules; correction; chastisement; the system by which a church orders its members.
GODLINESS, n. Piety; belief in God, with reverence and obedience to his commands; a religious life.
PRACTICE, n. Frequent or customary actions; a succession of acts of a similar kind; the exercise of a profession.
SABBATH, n. The day which God appointed to be observed by the Jews as a day of rest; the Lord's day among Christians.

Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world;

corruption_summary: Island province at the mouth of the Scheldt, first taken for the revolt in 1572, strictest of the Dutch provinces, and the cradle of the Nadere Reformatie at Middelburg.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the orthodoxy that is satisfied with being right, and Zeeland is where it was challenged from inside. The Dutch church after Dort had the best confession and the best canons in Europe, and Teellinck's complaint was that its members drank, swore, broke the Sabbath and neglected their households much as before. His answer was not a new doctrine but the application of the old one, which is what the apostle requires: “be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only” (Jam 1:22). A nation may hold the Canons of Dort and still need to be told that.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that grace teaches a manner of living and not only a scheme of salvation. “denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world” (Tit 2:12) is the Nadere Reformatie's whole text, and the call is to holiness in the ordinary conduct of a household: “be ye holy in all manner of conversation” (1Pe 1:15). Zeeland's ministers were also plain that pressing this would cost them, since “all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution” (2Ti 3:12) is true inside a Reformed republic as well as under Spain.

pos: n. (the northern Dutch province of a separate tongue, which produced Menno Simons and the university of Franeker)
etymology: Dutch Friesland, the land of the Frisians; the Frisian language is distinct from Dutch and closest of all continental tongues to English.
biblical_def: Friesland is the Dutch province that spoke its own language and went its own way in the Reformation, and it produced both the most influential Anabaptist of the century and one of the republic's two great Reformed faculties. Menno Simons was a Frisian parish priest at Witmarsum who, examining the mass and then infant baptism against the New Testament, left his living in 1536 and spent twenty-five years gathering the peaceable Anabaptists out of the wreck of the Munster rising, teaching nonresistance, a disciplined congregation and believers' baptism. The dictionary records his repudiation of Munster's violence as a real service and dissents from his view of the sacrament and of the magistrate. Reformed Friesland was organised by preachers trained abroad, among them Johannes Acronius, and in 1585 the province founded the university of Franeker, which for two centuries taught Reformed theology to Dutch, German, Hungarian and Scottish students, and whose Hebrew and covenant theology shaped the Hungarian and Scottish ministries as much as its own. Leeuwarden was its capital and Harlingen its port. The dictionary enters Friesland because a small province with its own speech and no great wealth furnished Europe with a theological faculty and the Mennonites with their name.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines nonresistance as the omission of resistance to power; a faculty as the professors of a science in a university; a parish as the precinct of a minister's charge; and baptism as the application of water as a sacrament.
webster_full: NONRESISTANCE, n. The omission of resistance; passive obedience; submission to authority, power or usurpation without opposition.
FACULTY, n. The body of professors or masters in a university, or in one of its departments of learning.
PARISH, n. The precinct or territorial jurisdiction of a secular priest, or the precinct the inhabitants of which belong to the same church.
BAPTISM, n. The application of water to a person, as a sacrament or religious ceremony, by which he is initiated into the visible church.
TONGUE, n. The language spoken by a particular nation; speech; the power of speaking.

corruption_summary: Northern Dutch province of a separate tongue, birthplace of Menno Simons and seat of the university of Franeker, founded 1585.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the violent sectarianism of Munster, which Menno Simons spent his life repudiating and which is still laid at the Anabaptists' door as though he had not. The men who seized Munster in 1534 claimed revelation, took the sword and ended in massacre; Menno answered them from the text, teaching that the Lord's people do not avenge themselves, since it is written “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord” (Rom 12:19). The dictionary holds his baptismal doctrine to be wrong and holds that on this point he was right, and that the distinction is owed him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the trained, examined ministry that a small province can still afford, which is what Franeker was. “Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed” (2Ti 2:15) was its charter in practice, and the Hungarians and Scots who studied there carried it home. Friesland's own people were commended for the Berean habit, that they “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11), which is how a Frisian priest came to leave his living in 1536.

pos: n. (the eastern Dutch duchy, last of the seven to join the revolt, where Veluanus wrote the first Reformed handbook in Dutch)
etymology: Dutch Gelderland, the land of Gelre, from the town of Geldern on the Niers; the duchy of Guelders in English usage.
biblical_def: Gelderland was a duchy rather than a county, inland, agricultural and divided into four quarters whose towns, Nijmegen, Arnhem, Zutphen and Tiel, pulled in different directions, and it was the last of the seven northern provinces to come fully into the revolt. Its importance in a Reformed dictionary rests on one book. Jan Gerritsz Versteghe, a parish priest of Garderen in the Veluwe who wrote under the name Johannes Anastasius Veluanus, was imprisoned for evangelical preaching and in 1554 published from his confinement Der Leken Wechwyser, the layman's guide: a handbook of Reformed doctrine in plain Dutch for people with no Latin, treating Scripture, justification, the sacraments, the saints and purgatory, and written for a reader who had never seen a theological book. It went through many printings and was for a generation the most widely read Protestant book in Dutch, doing in the Low Countries what Luther's catechism did in Germany. Gelderland afterwards built a Reformed church order like its neighbours, and Harderwijk eventually had a small academy. The dictionary enters Gelderland because its one great contribution was a book written for laymen by a prisoner, which is a more ordinary way for doctrine to spread than a university.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a layman as one not a clergyman; a handbook as a manual; a quarter as a fourth part or a district; and a guide as one who directs another in his way.
webster_full: LAYMAN, n. A man not a clergyman; one of the laity or people distinct from the clergy.
MANUAL, n. A small book, such as may be carried in the hand or conveniently handled.
QUARTER, n. The fourth part; a region of a town or country; a particular district or division.
GUIDE, n. A person who leads or directs another in his way; a director; a regulator.
PRISON, n. A place of confinement, or involuntary restraint; a jail.

corruption_summary: Eastern Dutch duchy, last of the seven to join the revolt, where the imprisoned Veluanus published the first Reformed handbook in plain Dutch in 1554.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the doctrine kept in a learned language, which Gelderland's one famous book was written to break. Veluanus wrote for a man who had no Latin and no library, taking each disputed head in order and answering it from the text in the speech of the Veluwe. The reproach made against such books is that they are not scholarship; the reply is that they are the ordinary instrument by which God teaches the simple, for “the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple” (Psa 19:7).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that teaching aims at the understanding of the hearer, whoever he is. “and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8) is the standard, and a layman's guide written in a cell meets it. The circumstances are worth recording with the book: the author was a prisoner, and the apostle's word fits him, that though he was bound “the word of God is not bound” (2Ti 2:9). The promise over such work is that “The meek will he guide in judgment” (Psa 25:9).

pos: n. (the Dutch province beyond the Ijssel, home of the Brethren of the Common Life whose schools taught the generation that reformed Europe)
etymology: Dutch Overijssel, the land over or beyond the river Ijssel; its three chief towns are Deventer, Zwolle and Kampen.
biblical_def: Overijssel is the province in which the Reformation's schoolmasters were trained a century before the Reformation. Along the Ijssel, at Deventer, Zwolle and Windesheim, Geert Groote and his followers gathered from the 1380s the Brethren of the Common Life: houses of clergy and laymen living in common without vows, copying books, teaching boys, and pressing a religion of inward devotion and the reading of Scripture against the formality of the age. Thomas a Kempis was of Zwolle's house and Wessel Gansfort of Groningen taught among them. Their schools, Deventer's above all, educated Erasmus and a whole generation of northern humanists, and their devotional method, plain, text-centred and suspicious of ceremony, prepared ground the Reformation later reaped. The dictionary dissents from their theology, which was monastic in its instincts, left justification unreformed, and in the Imitation teaches a self-abasement without a clear word of free justification. It records what they did: they taught boys Latin and Scripture cheaply, and they made books. Overijssel afterwards became Reformed, and Kampen later housed a seminary of the Dutch churches. The dictionary enters Overijssel because the Reformation did not arise out of nothing, and the Ijssel schools are much of the something.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines devotion as the state of being dedicated to God; a vow as a solemn promise made to God; imitation as the act of copying; and a scribe as a writer or copyist.
webster_full: DEVOTION, n. The state of being dedicated, consecrated or solemnly set apart for a particular purpose; piety; religious ardor.
VOW, n. A solemn promise made to God, or by a pagan to his deity; a solemn engagement to do something.
IMITATION, n. The act of copying; attempt to resemble; that which is offered as a copy.
SCRIBE, n. A writer; a notary; a public writer; one who transcribes or copies.
COMMON, a. Belonging equally to more than one, or to many indefinitely; usual; general.

corruption_summary: Dutch province beyond the Ijssel where the Brethren of the Common Life kept schools and copied books from the 1380s, teaching the generation that reformed Europe.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the piety that aims at inwardness and never reaches justification. The Brethren were serious men who taught boys to read Scripture and to despise display, and the Imitation of Christ is the most widely read devotional book ever produced in the Netherlands. It also leaves a reader working at his own abasement with no clear word that “a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28). The dictionary honours the schools and the presses, and says plainly that the doctrine wanted was supplied later and from elsewhere.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the teaching of children in the Scriptures, which the Ijssel houses did better than the universities of their day. Timothy is the pattern, that “from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures” (2Ti 3:15), and Deventer's school did that for boys whose fathers could not pay much. The limit of the method is the rule it never applied to itself: “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) would have tried the mass and the vows as well as the ceremonies, and the Brethren stopped short of trying them.

pos: n. (the central duchy of the Low Countries, where the Reformation's first martyrs died and whose university condemned Luther first)
etymology: Latin Brabantia, from the Frankish bracha, newly broken land, and bant, a district; the duchy held Brussels, Antwerp, Louvain and Bois-le-Duc.
biblical_def: Brabant is the duchy in which the Reformation was first condemned and first paid for in blood. Louvain, its university, was the earliest faculty in Europe to censure Luther, publishing its condemnation in November 1519 before Rome had finished its own process, and its theologians afterwards drew up the indexes of forbidden books for the Netherlands. Brussels, its chief residence, was where the Augustinians Hendrik Voes and Jan van Esch were burned on 1 July 1523, the first men executed anywhere for Reformation doctrine; their house at Antwerp was suppressed and its prior imprisoned. Antwerp itself, Brabant's port and for a generation the richest city in northern Europe, was the Low Countries' printing capital and its most mixed population, Lutheran, Calvinist, Anabaptist and Catholic at once, until the Spanish recapture of 1585 drove its Protestants north. Brabant was divided by the war: the north became Dutch and largely remained Catholic in population, the south stayed with Spain. The dictionary enters Brabant because the firsts belong here. The first censure, the first index, the first martyrs and the first great Protestant press were all in one duchy, and the Reformation's opponents moved faster in it than anywhere else.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an index as a table of contents or a list of prohibited books; to censure as to blame or condemn; a faculty as the body of professors; and a prior as the superior of a convent.
webster_full: INDEX, n. A table of contents; among the Romanists, a catalogue of prohibited books.
CENSURE, v. To find fault with and condemn as wrong; to blame; to express disapprobation of.
FACULTY, n. The body of professors or masters in a university, or in one of its departments of learning.
PRIOR, n. The superior of a convent of monks, or one next in dignity to an abbot.
STAKE, n. A small piece of wood sharpened at one end; the post to which one condemned to be burnt was fastened.

And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held:

They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented;
corruption_summary: Central duchy of the Low Countries, whose university at Louvain condemned Luther in 1519 and whose capital burned the first Reformation martyrs in 1523.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the index, the list of books a people may not read, of which Louvain's theologians were the Netherlands' principal authors. An index assumes what the Reformation denied, that the laity must be protected from the text by men who have it; and it is answered not by a counter-list but by the apostles' reply when they were forbidden to teach, “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29). Brabant's indexes were enforced with real severity, and Antwerp's printers went on working anyway.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the martyr's blessing is attached to the cause and not to the quantity. Two Augustinians died at Brussels in 1523, which is a small number beside the thousands who followed them, and the word over them is the same: “Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake” (Mat 5:10). They are the first of the company seen “under the altar” (Rev 6:9) in the Low Countries, and the dictionary notes that their own faculty at Louvain had supplied the sentence four years before the fire was lit.

pos: n. (the French-speaking county of the southern Low Countries, which led the Catholic Union of Arras in 1579 and broke the Seventeen Provinces)
etymology: French Artois, from the Atrebates, the Gallic people of the region; its capital is Arras, Flemish Atrecht.
biblical_def: Artois is the county whose decision divided the Low Countries permanently. French-speaking, agricultural, strongly Catholic in its nobility and clergy, and bordering France, it had little of the trade and less of the Reformed preaching that marked Flanders and Holland; its one great Protestant name is Louis de Berquin, a gentleman of Artois who was burned at Paris in 1529 as the first French noble martyr of the Reformation. When the revolt against Spain turned Calvinist in temper and the Reformed took control of Ghent and other Flemish towns by force, the Catholic nobility of the south, who had joined the revolt to recover their privileges and not to change their religion, drew back. On 6 January 1579 Artois, Hainaut and Lille concluded the Union of Arras, declaring for the king and the old religion; three weeks later the northern provinces answered with the Union of Utrecht. From that pair of documents came the permanent division of the Low Countries into the Dutch republic and the Spanish Netherlands, which is to say the border of Belgium. The dictionary enters Artois because the split was caused as much by the Reformed party's coercion in Flanders as by Spanish arms, and that is worth saying plainly.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a union as a confederacy or league; a privilege as a peculiar advantage; coercion as restraint by force; and a county as a district governed by a count.
webster_full: UNION, n. A league or confederacy; the junction of two or more states or provinces for a common purpose.
PRIVILEGE, n. A particular and peculiar benefit or advantage enjoyed by a person, company or society.
COERCION, n. Restraint, check, particularly by law or authority; compulsion; force.
COUNTY, n. Originally, an earldom; a district or portion of a kingdom governed by a count or earl.
BORDER, n. The outer edge of anything; the exterior limit of a country or region; a frontier.

Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.
Mat 5:10
Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
corruption_summary: French-speaking county of the southern Low Countries which concluded the Catholic Union of Arras in 1579 and so fixed the border between the Dutch republic and the Spanish Netherlands.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the advancing of the Reformed cause by force on its own side, and Artois is the bill for it. In 1577 and 1578 the Calvinist parties in Ghent and other Flemish towns seized the churches, suppressed the mass and treated Catholic magistrates as enemies; the Catholic nobility of the south, who had been in the revolt from the beginning, concluded they were safer with the king, and signed at Arras. Weapons of that kind were never given to the church, for “the weapons of our warfare are not carnal” (2Co 10:4), and the sword taken up at Ghent cost the Reformation ten provinces.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the gospel is to be commended to a neighbour who differs, so far as it depends on us: “live peaceably with all men” (Rom 12:18) is an apostolic command and not a counsel of weakness. The warning given in the garden applies to a Calvinist as to a Spaniard, that “all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52). Artois also has its martyr, and the dictionary names him: Louis de Berquin, burned in 1529, of whom it may be said he was “persecuted for righteousness' sake” (Mat 5:10).

pos: n. (the Walloon county where Guido de Bres ministered and where the Belgic Confession was written in 1561)
etymology: French Hainaut, Dutch Henegouwen, from the river Haine and the Germanic gouwe, a district; its capital is Mons.
biblical_def: Hainaut is the Walloon county that gave the Reformed churches of the Low Countries their confession. Its towns, Mons, Valenciennes and Tournai on its border, lay close enough to France to be fed by French books and French preachers, and from the 1540s they held some of the most determined Reformed congregations in the Netherlands, meeting in fields and quarries and known for singing psalms in the streets, which the authorities of Valenciennes in 1562 treated as insurrection. Guido de Bres, a glass-painter's son of Mons, trained at Lausanne and Geneva and minister to these congregations, wrote in 1561 the Confession of Faith of the Reformed Churches of the Low Countries, the Belgic Confession, and a copy was thrown over the wall of Tournai castle with an address to Philip II protesting the congregations' loyalty in all civil things and their refusal to yield in religion. The Confession was adopted by the Synod of Emden in 1571 and by Dort, and remains a standard of the Dutch and Belgian Reformed churches. De Bres was hanged at Valenciennes on 31 May 1567. The dictionary enters Hainaut because its confession was written by a working pastor for a hunted people and addressed to the king who was hunting them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a confession as a formulary of the articles of faith; loyalty as fidelity to a prince; a quarry as a place where stones are dug; and a psalm as a sacred song or hymn.
webster_full: CONFESSION, n. A formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised; a profession of belief.
LOYALTY, n. Fidelity to a prince or sovereign, or to a husband or lover; fidelity to a lawful government.
QUARRY, n. A place, cavern or pit where stones are dug from the earth, or separated from a large mass of rocks.
PSALM, n. A sacred song or hymn; a song composed on a divine subject and in praise of God.
GALLOWS, n. An instrument of punishment, whereon criminals are executed by hanging.

Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
Psa 96:3
Declare his glory among the heathen, his wonders among all people.
And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.
corruption_summary: Walloon county where Guido de Bres served the hunted Reformed congregations, wrote the Belgic Confession in 1561, and was hanged at Valenciennes in 1567.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the charge of sedition laid against men who were not seditious, and Hainaut is where the Reformed answered it most carefully. The congregations of Valenciennes and Mons were accused of rebellion for assembling and for singing psalms; the Belgic Confession was written and delivered to the king precisely to show that they held civil obedience to be a duty of religion and asked only not to be required to sin. The two commands stand together: “Honour the king” (1Pe 2:17) in all that is his, and “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) where the two collide.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a confession is a public act of witness, meant to be read by magistrates and not only by synods. De Bres wrote his for a king and was hanged by that king's officers six years later, which is the ordinary cost of such plainness, and of him the word holds that they “loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11). The psalm-singing the authorities feared was simply the command obeyed: “Declare his glory among the heathen” (Psa 96:3).

pos: n. (the Dutch republic's great city, which turned Reformed in a single day in 1578 and became the printing house and refuge of Protestant Europe)
etymology: Dutch Amsterdam, the dam on the Amstel; the town grew from a thirteenth-century fishing settlement at the river's mouth.
biblical_def: Amsterdam became the chief city of the Dutch republic and the most useful city in Europe to the Protestant cause, chiefly because it printed and because it let people in. It stayed Catholic and loyal to Spain longer than its neighbours, and on 26 May 1578 its Catholic council and clergy were removed in a bloodless municipal revolution, the Alteration, after which the city was Reformed and its churches were handed to Reformed ministers. What followed was not uniformity but a working toleration unusual in that age: the public church was Reformed and officeholders had to belong to it, while Mennonites, Lutherans, Remonstrants, Roman Catholics and the Portuguese and German Jews held their worship in private houses and hidden churches which everybody knew about. The English Separatists came, and Amsterdam is where John Smyth and Henry Ainsworth's congregations argued out the questions that produced the first English Baptists; the Pilgrims passed through on their way to Leiden. Its presses printed in every language of Europe what was forbidden at home, Bibles among the rest. The dictionary enters Amsterdam because the republic's most commercial city was also its most hospitable one, and because the hospitality was not a theory of liberty but a habit of not asking.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines alteration as the act of making different; a refuge as shelter or protection from danger; toleration as the allowance of religious opinions; and a stranger as a foreigner or sojourner.
webster_full: ALTERATION, n. The act of making different, or of varying in some particular; a change; the state of being altered.
REFUGE, n. Shelter or protection from danger or distress; that which shelters or protects from danger.
TOLERATION, n. The allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state, when contrary to the established church.
STRANGER, n. A foreigner; one who belongs to another country; one not a citizen; a guest.
HOSPITALITY, n. The act or practice of receiving and entertaining strangers or guests without reward.
scriptures: Heb 13:2
Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
But the stranger that dwelleth with you shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God.
Use hospitality one to another without grudging.
For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in:
corruption_summary: Chief city of the Dutch republic, turned Reformed by the Alteration of 26 May 1578, and the printing house and refuge of Protestant Europe.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the grudging reception of refugees, measured by what they cost rather than by what is commanded. Amsterdam received Walloons, Flemings, English Separatists, French Huguenots, German Lutherans and Sephardi Jews, partly from charity and partly because they brought trades and capital, and the dictionary does not pretend the second motive was absent. It records that the command stands on its own ground: “Use hospitality one to another without grudging” (1Pe 4:9), and a city which obeys it for mixed reasons has still obeyed it, while a city which refuses on pure ones has not.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the duty of welcome which the law laid on Israel and the gospel lays on the church. “the stranger that dwelleth with you shall be unto you as one born among you” (Lev 19:34) is the old statute, and “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers” (Heb 13:2) is its renewal. Amsterdam's hidden churches were a compromise and not a settled liberty, and the dictionary says so; they were also the reason the first English Baptist congregation had somewhere to meet and argue, and “I was a stranger, and ye took me in” (Mat 25:35) is what the Lord calls that.
